subject: Marine Science

outcomes.text: Understand how substances dissolve in water.
Explain solute, solvent, solution and solubility.
Describe how soluble salts dissolve in water through separation of their ions.
Explain how water temperature affects salt solubility.
Define salinity as dissolved-salt concentration in seawater, measured in parts per thousand.
Investigate how salinity changes water’s freezing point.
Explain how runoff, precipitation and evaporation alter seawater salinity.
Describe pH as a measure of hydrogen-ion concentration and distinguish acidic, neutral and alkaline water.
Use indicators and pH probes to identify acidity or alkalinity and measure water-sample pH.
State that oxygen dissolves only slightly in water.
Describe how temperature, depth-related pressure, atmospheric pressure and salinity affect gas solubility and marine organisms.
Understand density and pressure in marine environments.
Explain how temperature, pressure and salinity affect seawater density.
Apply density equals mass divided by volume, using appropriate SI units.
State that ice is less dense than seawater and therefore floats.
Explain floating ice’s importance as thermal insulation and marine-organism habitat.
Describe how temperature and salinity gradients create ocean layers and how those layers subsequently mix.
Explain water’s solid, liquid and gaseous states using kinetic particle theory.
Describe atoms as nuclei containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons arranged in shells.
Understand that seawater contains a mixture of different elements and compounds.
Describe covalent bonding in water as atoms sharing electron pairs, including with diagrams.
Identify covalent molecules, including water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, sulfur dioxide and glucose.
Describe sodium chloride’s ionic bonding through electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Identify ionic substances, including sodium chloride and calcium carbonate.
State names and formulae for seawater salts, including sodium chloride, magnesium sulfate and calcium carbonate.
Explain how hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
Explain how hydrogen bonding affects water’s solvent action, density and specific heat capacity.
Understand weathering, erosion and sedimentation in marine settings.
Distinguish weathering from erosion.
Describe chemical, physical and organic weathering, giving an example of each.
Describe erosion by ice, water, wind and gravity.
Describe sedimentation as deposition of suspended particles.
Explain how water-flow speed and particle size affect particle removal, transport and deposition.
Define the littoral zone as the intertidal area between highest and lowest spring-tide marks.
Give examples of littoral environments, including rocky, sandy and muddy shores, estuaries and deltas.
Describe how weathering, erosion and sedimentation shape rocky and sandy shores, muddy shores, estuaries and deltas.
Understand tides and ocean currents.
Explain tidal formation and how astronomical, coastal and atmospheric factors alter tidal range.
Explain how spring and neap tides form.
Interpret tide tables and graphs for height, range, spring tides and neap tides.
Describe how wind, temperature, density, Coriolis deflection and seabed shape create currents and upwelling.
Explain the global ocean conveyor belt and its role in circulating seawater.
Discuss causes and effects of El Niño and La Niña in the Pacific ENSO cycle.
Describe Earth’s crust, mantle and core, distinguishing oceanic from continental crust.
Describe and apply plate tectonic theory using geological, fossil, paleomagnetic and coastline evidence.
Identify convergent, divergent and transform plate boundaries and describe each type.
Explain how tectonics form trenches, ridges, vents, abyssal plains, volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis.
State that hydrothermal-vent water is pressurised, hot and nutrient-rich, forming a vent plume.
Understand that hydrothermal-vent plume effects can be detected away from the vent.
Explain vent-chimney formation using temperature changes and salt solubility.
Understand feeding relationships in marine ecosystems.
Explain key feeding-relationship terms, including consumers, producers, trophic levels, predators, prey and decomposers.
Represent and interpret ecosystem feeding relationships using food chains and food webs.
Understand that producers may use photosynthesis or chemosynthesis.
Explain how photosynthesis captures sunlight energy and summarise it with the word equation for glucose production.
Investigate how light intensity affects photosynthesis rate.
Understand that photosynthetic glucose can be used to build biomass.
Understand that glucose is used in respiration for usable energy and state its word equation.
Define productivity and explain how high primary productivity can affect food chains.
Calculate and explain energy losses along food chains.
Draw, describe and interpret energy, numbers and biomass pyramids, including parasites and plankton blooms.
Understand nutrient cycles in marine ecosystems.
Understand nutrients as substances needed for growth, repair, energy supply or normal metabolism.
Recognise nutrients as gases, ions or organic compounds.
State the elements composing carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
State how starch, cellulose, proteins and lipids are formed from smaller molecules.
Explain biological roles of nitrogen, carbon, magnesium, calcium and phosphorus.
Understand that soluble nutrients form an ocean reservoir available to producers and consumers.
Explain how upwelling, runoff, tectonics, atmospheric gases, excretion and decomposition replenish dissolved nutrients.
Understand that organisms deplete dissolved nutrients through uptake.
Understand that harvesting removes nutrients incorporated into organisms.
Outline how marine snow carries organic, energy-rich material from surface waters to the deep ocean.
Explain why dissolved-nutrient availability can limit productivity.
Describe the carbon cycle, including combustion, photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, fossil fuels and carbonate rocks.
Define parasitism, commensalism and mutualism as types of symbiotic relationship.
Understand that different species can live closely together in symbiotic relationships, including parasitism, commensalism and mutualism.
Describe parasitism using copepods and marine fish as an example.
Describe commensalism using whales and barnacles as an example.
Describe mutualism using boxer crabs and anemones as an example.
Recognise the key groups of marine organisms.
Define plankton as mostly microscopic organisms with limited movement that drift with water currents.
Understand that phytoplankton photosynthesise, absorb environmental nutrients and act as producers.
Understand that zooplankton are consumers, including larvae, copepods and jellyfish.
State the characteristic features of adult echinoderms: five-part radial symmetry and tube feet.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of echinoderms, including crown-of-thorns starfish.
State crustacean features including a carapace, segmented abdomen, jointed legs and two antenna pairs.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of crustaceans, including Antarctic krill.
State the main internal and external features of adult bony fish, including skeleton, operculum, gills, swim bladder, scales, lateral line and fins.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of bony fish, including Peruvian anchoveta.
State the main internal and external features of adult cartilaginous fish, including skeleton, gill structures, denticles, lateral line and fins.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of cartilaginous fish, including blue sharks.
Understand that both fish groups are chordates sharing features such as a notochord, dorsal neural tube, pharyngeal slits and post-anal tail.
State the main features of macroalgae such as kelp, including holdfast, stipe, gas bladders and blades.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of macroalgae, including kelp.
State the main features of marine plants such as seagrass, including rhizomes, roots, flowers and leaves.
Understand the ecological and economic significance of marine plants, including seagrass.
Understand biodiversity in marine environments.
Explain biodiversity at genetic, species and ecological levels.
Understand marine biodiversity benefits, including ecosystem stability, environmental protection, climate regulation, food and medicines.
Understand marine populations and sampling techniques.
Explain ecosystem, habitat, niche, species, population and community using marine examples.
Explain biotic and abiotic factors and identify their effects on organisms in a named marine ecosystem.
Understand mark–release–recapture for estimating the size of a named species’ population.
Apply the Lincoln index and identify limitations of this population estimate.
Describe random and systematic sampling, including their strengths and weaknesses.
Use quadrats, transects and mark–release–recapture to investigate littoral organism distribution and abundance safely and ethically.
Calculate habitat species diversity with Simpson’s index and interpret differing index values.
Use Spearman’s rank correlation to analyse relationships between species distribution or abundance and environmental factors.
Describe the taxonomic hierarchy from domain through kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Understand and apply binomial naming for species.
Construct and use simple dichotomous keys using readily observable characteristics.
Make observations and drawings of unfamiliar specimens or structures from specified marine organism groups.
Understand the characteristics of tropical coral reef ecosystems.
Describe environmental conditions needed for tropical coral reef formation.
Describe and compare fringing, barrier, patch and atoll reefs by coastal position and lagoon structure.
Describe corals as cnidarian animals forming sessile polyp colonies, often with zooxanthellae symbiosis.
Understand how hard and soft corals differ in calcification and zooxanthellae abundance.
Describe hard-coral polyp structures and explain their functions.
Explain coral nutrition, including mutualism between some coral polyps and zooxanthellae.
Discuss coral reef importance for tourism, food, coastal protection, medicines and biodiversity.
Discuss causes and effects of reef erosion, including acidity, temperature, predation, physical damage and sediment.
Discuss applications of artificial reefs.
Understand the characteristics of rocky shore ecosystems.
Identify rocky-shore zones and describe changing abiotic conditions through a tidal cycle.
Explain how biological and physical factors affect organism distribution and abundance across rocky-shore zones.
Explain, with named examples, adaptations enabling organisms to live in different rocky-shore zones.
Understand the characteristics of sandy shore ecosystems.
Describe sandy shores as porous ecosystems with unstable, shifting substrates.
Explain why sandy-shore conditions produce relatively low biodiversity.
Investigate how particle size affects substrate permeability.
Explain, with named examples, adaptations for living on sandy shores.
Understand the characteristics of mangrove forest ecosystems.
Describe mangrove forests as tidal communities of salt-tolerant plants and other interacting species.
Outline conditions needed for mangrove forest formation.
Explain red mangrove adaptations, including prop roots, salt exclusion and viviparous propagule reproduction.
Explain mangrove ecological roles in providing nurseries and trapping sediment that protects coasts and nearby habitats.
Discuss mangrove importance for tourism, food, coastal protection, timber, fuel and biodiversity.
Discuss threats to mangroves, including temperature change, overharvesting, storms and altered coastal land use.
Identify the five oceans and understand their connections as one global ocean.
Identify open-ocean depth zones and describe them by light penetration.
Explain ocean interactions with the atmosphere through carbon storage, oxygen production, temperature buffering and climate regulation.
Identify polar, temperate and tropical ocean regions.
Understand how substances move into, out of and within marine organisms.
Describe and explain diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Explain water potential and how dissolved solutes alter the water potential of solutions and cells.
Investigate diffusion and osmosis using plant tissue and non-living materials.
Calculate surface area and volume for simple shapes and use these to demonstrate changing surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Investigate how changing surface-area-to-volume ratio affects diffusion through differently sized agar blocks.
Investigate plant tissues in solutions with different water potentials and estimate tissue water potential.
Explain water movement between differing water potentials and its effects on plant and animal cells.
Understand gas exchange in marine organisms.
Understand that respiratory reactants and waste products must travel to and from an organism’s surface.
Relate surface-area-to-volume ratio to organism size and the need for specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.
Describe gas exchange by diffusion, pumped ventilation and ram ventilation in coral polyps, grouper and tuna.
Relate an organism’s gas-exchange method to its habitat and movement.
Understand how marine organisms regulate water and solute balance.
Explain why marine organisms regulate water and ion content using comparisons of seawater and body fluids.
Explain osmoconformers and osmoregulators using marine mussels and tuna as examples.
Distinguish euryhaline and stenohaline organisms using salmon, marine mussels and tuna.
Outline osmoregulatory processes in salmon.
Identify listed organelles and cell structures, and summarise the function of each.
Describe the fluid mosaic membrane model, including phospholipids, carrier proteins and channel proteins.
Explain selective permeability and distinguish passive and active transport across membranes.
Describe and interpret images and drawings of typical animal and plant cells.
Apply the formula magnification equals image size divided by actual size.
Observe unfamiliar specimens or structures, draw them, and calculate their magnification.
Understand chemosynthesis as a source of biological energy.
Describe chemosynthesis as carbon fixation powered by chemical energy from substances such as sulfide, methane, hydrogen or iron.
Explain how vent bacteria provide usable energy that supports food chains.
Describe the symbiosis between Riftia tubeworms and Endoriftia bacteria.
Explain how Endoriftia uses hydrogen sulfide to fix carbon and produce organic compounds.
Understand respiration and energy release in marine organisms.
Understand aerobic respiration as oxygen-dependent ATP production from organic nutrients.
Represent aerobic respiration with word and chemical equations.
Explain that anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is limited and produces less ATP per glucose molecule.
Describe mitochondrial matrix, outer membrane and inner membrane folds called cristae.
State the cellular locations of aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Understand that white light contains colours with different wavelengths.
Distinguish wavelength, intensity and penetration when discussing light.
Describe how wavelength affects light penetration at different depths.
Explain photosynthetic carbon fixation by marine producers and represent it with a balanced equation.
Understand that photosynthesis has light-dependent and light-independent stages.
Explain how ATP and reduced NADP transfer energy between photosynthetic stages to make organic compounds.
Describe the main structures of a chloroplast, including membranes, stroma, thylakoids, spaces and grana.
State where the light-dependent and light-independent reactions occur in chloroplasts.
Describe how chlorophyll a and accessory pigments absorb light in grana.
Relate marine producers’ accessory pigments to absorption of wavelengths penetrating different depths.
Use chromatography and Rf values to separate and identify chloroplast pigments.
Interpret pigment absorption spectra and photosynthesis action spectra.
Describe light-dependent reactions as chlorophyll activation, water splitting and energy transfer to ATP and reduced NADP.
Describe Calvin-cycle carbon fixation using rubisco, ATP and reduced NADP to form organic molecules.
Explain how light, wavelength, carbon dioxide and temperature limit photosynthetic rate.
Investigate how light wavelength affects photosynthetic rate.
Understand approaches to maintaining sustainable fisheries.
Explain why fisheries must be exploited sustainably, referring to a named marine organism.
Discuss how sonar, purse seines, benthic trawls and factory ships affect populations and habitats.
Describe information needed for sustainable exploitation, including recruitment, growth, mortality, maturity, fecundity and habitat dependence.
Outline management tools including seasonal, quota, licensing, location, method, size, intensity, monitoring, penalties and consumer measures.
Evaluate management tools for effectiveness and effects on non-target species.
Discuss short- and long-term social and economic effects of restricted and unrestricted fishing.
Evaluate stock-recovery strategies including mangrove restoration, artificial reefs and releasing cultivated organisms.
Understand marine aquaculture and its role in future fisheries.
Describe intensive and extensive aquaculture methods using named marine organisms.
Outline aquaculture processes for salmon, marine mussels and shrimp.
Explain requirements for successful long-term aquaculture projects, including stock, water, feed, labour, disease control, location and markets.
Discuss aquaculture effects such as habitat loss, pollution, escapes, disease, resource competition, reduced wild harvests and social or economic consequences.
Describe metamorphosis, larval stages, and sessile or mobile stages in marine animal life cycles.
Compare simple and complex life cycles using marine mammals and crustaceans, including larvae and metamorphosis.
Outline the importance of different life stages in sessile and mobile organisms.
Discuss internal and external fertilisation and parental investment, using tuna, sharks and whales.

units.title: [A Level] 9 Human impacts on marine ecosystems

outcomes.text: Understand ocean acidification and its effects on marine ecosystems.
Explain links between atmospheric and dissolved carbon dioxide, ocean acidity and the ocean’s role in regulating atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Describe carbon dioxide reactions in water, including hydrogen and hydrogen carbonate ion formation, and effects on pH and carbonate availability.
Describe how ocean acidification affects hard corals and organisms with shells.
Investigate how pH affects mass loss from empty mollusc shells.
Understand conservation of marine ecosystems.
Explain why conservation is needed to maintain or improve biodiversity.
Explain how the IUCN Red List helps prioritise marine conservation decisions at different scales.
Define invasive and endangered species according to IUCN terminology.
Explain why invasive species threaten native marine organisms and ecosystems.
Evaluate the feasibility of proposed conservation projects using supplied information.
Discuss conservation strategies including protected areas, captive breeding, legislation, reserves, marine facilities, ecotourism and invasive-species control.
Explain why large marine ecosystems require international cooperation and legislation, and assess consequences when participation is incomplete.
Explain how oil, agriculture, renewable energy, sewage, refuse, desalination and fishing affect marine quality, habitats, organisms and food webs.
Explain toxin accumulation within organisms and increasing concentrations through food chains, including metals from antifouling paint and fossil-fuel combustion.
Define microplastics as particles below 5 mm and distinguish primary from secondary microplastics.
Describe how plastics fragment through ultraviolet radiation, wind and waves, and explain temperature effects on this process.
Discuss ecological and human effects of plastics, including plankton uptake, food-chain transfer, toxins, ingestion and entanglement.
Discuss methods for reducing plastic and microplastic release into marine ecosystems.
Describe how the natural greenhouse effect maintains Earth’s ambient temperature.
Explain how an enhanced greenhouse effect causes global warming.
Describe evidence demonstrating global warming.
Evaluate evidence supporting and challenging significant human contribution to global warming.
Describe marine effects of warming, including sea-level rise, coral bleaching, species redistribution and altered ocean circulation.
